conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for coming in today. I’m Dr. Riley, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m here to support you during this huge life transition. Before we talk about how things are going, I’d like to do a quick check-in using a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s just 10 questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. It helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can pop up after childbirth, and it includes a question about self-harm so we can make sure you’re safe. Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space—there are no right or wrong answers, only your honest experience. When you’re ready, we’ll go through the questions one by one. 

Let’s start: Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Yeah… I’ve noticed I don’t really laugh much anymore. When my partner or my mom tries to joke around, I’ll give a little smile, but nothing feels funny inside. I used to laugh a lot—before the baby, even during pregnancy—but lately it just feels flat, like I don’t have the energy or the heart for it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I wish I could say that’s true for me, but… no, not really. I might force a little chuckle if someone else is laughing, but it feels fake. Nothing seems genuinely funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

No… I can’t remember the last time I actually looked forward to anything. Even little outings—like meeting a friend for coffee or taking the baby for a walk—feel like chores. I used to get excited about the smallest plans, but now it’s just “get through it,” not enjoy it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him, I keep thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right or I missed some cue. Last night he wouldn’t sleep and I lay there wondering what I was doing wrong as a mom. Even when my partner says it’s normal, I still feel like it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my chest feels tight, thinking the baby might stop breathing in the next room, or that I’ll drop him when I pick him up. There’s no real reason—he’s healthy, the monitor’s on—but the thoughts just keep spinning.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… sometimes it hits me out of nowhere. Like yesterday, I was just warming up a bottle and suddenly my heart was racing and I felt this wave of dread, like something awful was about to happen. It lasted a few minutes, then faded, but it left me shaky. There wasn’t anything actually wrong—it’s like my body just flips into panic mode without warning.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. Feels like I’m drowning in bottles, laundry, diaper changes, and I can never catch up. When the baby finally naps, I think “great, now I can breathe,” but then I look around at the mess and my mind starts racing with everything I “should” be doing. I get this knot in my stomach that I’m failing at keeping it all together.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Exactly. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off—running through everything I did wrong that day or might mess up tomorrow. Some nights I’m still awake when the baby’s ready for the next feed, and then I’m too worked up to fall back asleep even after he settles.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… that’s most days now. I wake up with this heavy feeling, like there’s a weight on my chest. Sometimes I’ll just look at the baby and start crying because I feel so low, even though he’s not doing anything wrong. It’s like the sadness is just sitting there, and I can’t shake it off.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A few times this week, yeah. Yesterday I spilled some pumped milk and just sat on the floor and sobbed—it felt like the worst thing in the world, even though I knew it wasn’t. I tell myself it’s just hormones, but the tears keep coming whenever I’m stressed or feel like I’m failing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel overwhelmed and sad, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby needs.

You've shared how the joy you once found in small moments has been replaced by a heavy sadness and constant worry since your baby arrived. Laughing feels forced, outings feel like chores, and simple tasks can leave you in tears. Most mornings you wake with a weight on your chest, nights are spent running through everything you think you're doing wrong, and panic can appear out of nowhere while you warm a bottle. Yet you've also made it clear that you want to feel better so you can be the mom your baby deserves, and that desire for relief and connection is an important source of hope.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports complete inability to find things genuinely funny, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing even small plans as burdensome chores, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame ('do that a lot') across multiple situations, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-constant, intrusive, catastrophic worries despite objective safety, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Her description of sudden racing heart and dread that arises "out of nowhere" and leaves her shaky clearly aligns with experiencing panic symptoms "sometimes."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to keep up with daily tasks, racing thoughts, and a sense of failure—closely matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia driven by distressing ruminations, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness most days, waking with heaviness, spontaneous crying, and inability to shake the low mood—clearly aligns with "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes triggered by minor stressors, indicating "quite often" level of distress.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 on the EPDS falls well above the 14-point cutoff for probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>, indicating severe symptom burden. Her responses map onto core DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset: depressed mood most days (<sym>weight on chest</sym>), markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>nothing feels funny</sym>, <sym>no enjoyment in outings</sym>), feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt (<sym>blaming myself unnecessarily</sym>), concentration difficulties (<sym>brain won't shut off</sym>), and insomnia. In addition, recurrent <sym>panic-like episodes</sym> and near-constant <sym>anxiety</sym> suggest a likely comorbid <med>anxiety disorder</med>. No self-harm ideation is endorsed, so acute safety risk is lower, but severity of mood and functional impairment warrant urgent assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist to confirm diagnosis and discuss antidepressant options compatible with breastfeeding if applicable
2. Request referral to a perinatal therapist trained in CBT or interpersonal therapy for <med>postpartum depression</med> and <med>anxiety</med> to build coping and self-compassion skills
3. Mobilize support: ask partner, family, or friends to handle night feeds once per night and household tasks so you can obtain 4-5 hours of uninterrupted sleep; adequate rest is a first-line intervention
4. Practice brief daily self-care: 10-minute stroller walk outside or guided breathing audio when baby naps-tiny, scheduled activities can gradually restore pleasure pathways
5. Monitor mood daily using a phone app or journal; bring log to your provider visit to guide medication or therapy adjustments
6. Keep emergency resources handy: 24/7 Postpartum Support International text line 800-944-4773 and local urgent mental-health hotline if symptoms escalate
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary**

**Chief concerns reported:**  
- Persistent low mood, daily tearfulness, and inability to experience pleasure  
- Marked loss of interest/enjoyment in previously rewarding activities  
- Pervasive guilt/self-blame regarding parenting performance  
- Frequent, unprovoked anxiety, panic symptoms, and catastrophic worries about infant safety  
- Sleep disturbance driven by rumination and mood distress  
- Feeling overwhelmed and “drowning” in routine tasks  

**Pattern highlights:**  
- All items consistent with depressed mood and anhedonia (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Elevated generalized and panic-type anxiety without identifiable triggers (Q4, Q5)  
- Excessive guilt/feelings of inadequacy, typical of perinatal mood disorders (Q3)  
- Functional impact: difficulty coping with daily infant care and household demands (Q6)  
- Insomnia secondary to mood rather than infant schedule (Q7)  

**Risk considerations:**  
- Moderate to high alignment with probable postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety; patient endorses sadness, guilt, anhedonia, crying spells, and impaired functioning  
- No suicidal ideation or self-harm intent reported (Q10) → **not a current acute safety concern**  

**Screening impression:**  
Patient’s responses indicate clinically significant postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms warranting prompt formal evaluation and possible referral for perinatal mental health services.
